# Linking Your Thinking (LYT)

Linking Your Thinking (LYT) is a framework for personal knowledge management (PKM) created by Nick Milo. According to Milo, it uses links between notes to improve thinking, and it equips a digital note library with a small set of flexible structures: a Home Note, Maps of Content and other Fluid Frameworks (LYT). The collection of linked notes that results is called an Ideaverse.

## Core idea
- LYT is optional scaffolding on top of ordinary notes. A beginner can simply write notes; Milo suggests coming back to the structures after roughly 100 notes, when favourite notes become hard to find and the urge to build a map appears (see Mental Squeeze Point (LYT)).
- Structure should be earned and emerge from use, not designed up front. Milo warns people who tend to over-organize not to build an "ultimate" system on day one.
- LYT is not the same as a zettelkasten. Milo says a zettelkasten is narrowly about writing for output, while LYT extends it to anything that involves thinking and writing.
- The three thinking modes: top-down (start from structure), bottom-up (start from ideas) and middle-out (a fluid structure that cycles between both), which Milo associates with LYT.

## Guiding values
Milo proposes that a digital library should be a joy to use, future-proof, fast to search today and in ten years, encouraging of active, lateral and generative thinking, open to cross-pollination of ideas, able to produce finished work, and cumulative: it should gain meaning and personal value over time and reward repetition. Its guiding questions are: can I find things quickly, can I think fast and deeply, and can I be surprised by serendipitous connections?

## Benefits claimed for linked frameworks
Milo lists: reliable home bases when thoughts waver; flexibility (frameworks curate access rather than limit it); a kick-start for the brain; more routes for retrieving a note; relief from overwhelm; relational and positional thinking; ready-made contexts to attach new notes to; and being able to return to a library after months away without anxiety. He also credits them with better recall through repetition, conceptual thinking and spatial context.

## Mentioned but not summarized
Milo also refers to the ARC framework (Add, Relate, Communicate) and to a paid workshop (the LYT Workshop) as the place where these are taught in depth. The kit does not describe either well enough to summarize here. Related terms: PKM is the process of making, using, organizing, connecting and creating with personal notes; see Personal Knowledge Management (LYT) for Milo's fuller account.

> [!contradiction] Naming of the MOC middle phase
> The kit names the middle MOC phase "Collide" in the walkthrough and "develop" in the FAQ and glossary. They are treated here as the same phase; see Maps of Content.
